newsitem.title: FRANCE: Russia to pay French holders of tsarist debts.
newsitem.headline: Russia to pay French holders of tsarist debts.

text.p: Russia signed an deal with France on Tuesday to compensate French holders of tsarist debt issued by Moscow before 1917, settling a dispute between the two nations.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe told a news conference the accord, reached in talks in Paris with visiting Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, covered payments of $400 million over several years. He did not elaborate.
The amount is a tiny fraction of the 140 to 160 billion francs ($27 to $31 billion) claimed by the French holders of tsarist bonds, mostly interest for the past 70 years.
Moscow has settled smaller debt disputes with holders of the bonds in Britain, the United States, Canada and Switzerland.
France's association of Russian debt holders, representing an estimated 400,000 people, denounced the accord as insufficient.
"There is no question of this being suitable payment. Instead it's merely symbolic," they said in a statement.

Chernomyrdin, on a two-day visit to France, said before leaving Moscow that Russia would pay the debt run up by its pre-1917 tsarist government and repudiated by the Soviet Union after the communist revolution.
The row over Moscow's tsarist debt has blocked trade in a new Russian bond in France.
The dispute marred Russia's return to international capital markets last week with an oversubscribed $1 billion Eurobond, its first debt offering since the 1917 revolution.
France banned trading in the Eurobond pending settlement of the compensation issue.

The dispute was also seen as an obstacle to Russia joining the powerful Paris Club of government creditors, which France chairs, a move that would allow it to negotiate the return of Soviet-era debts owed to Moscow, mainly by developing countries.
Speculation about Chernomyrdin's intentions had prompted the Paris bourse to suspend trade in the pre-revolutionary bonds.

An estimated 1.2 million French investors bought Russian bonds issued up to 1917 to fund projects like the Trans-Siberian railway. The bond holders' association estimates that 400,000 people hold them today.
The Soviet refusal to meet the obligations of its tsarist predecessor left savers holding virtually worthless, if attractively printed, paper.
Moscow has argued that any liability for Tsarist-era debt must be offset against the seizure in the West of Russian assets, which were used to help fight the Communists.

Chernomyrdin, who has been virtually running Russia while President Boris Yeltsin convalesces from heart bypass surgery on November 5, met conservative French President Jacques Chirac earlier on Tuesday.
At a joint news conference with Juppe, Chernomyrdin also reiterated his opposition to NATO expansion, saying Moscow considered the eastwards extension of the alliance a threat to its security.

Chirac spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said Chirac reiterated his desire for a summit including NATO states, eastern European nations who wish to join it and former Soviet republics, including Russia, as a preliminary step toward an agreement between NATO and Moscow.
"We understand that Russia remains worried and convinced that enlargement would constitute a threat to Russia's security," Colonna said.
